introduction: The Serbian Church of Saint George in central Pest was built in 1733 on the site of an older Serbian place of worship. It is the surviving centre of a Serbian community that settled in Pest after the Ottoman period.
chapters: Serbs in Pest under Ottoman and Habsburg rule

English Wikipedia records that a Serbian place of worship stood on the site during Ottoman rule, and that some sources suggest a church existed even before the Battle of Mohács in 1526. A source from 1655 records a separate cemetery beside the Kecskemét Gate, and between 1660 and 1664 the Ottoman traveller Evliya Çelebi noted that the Serbs of Pest had their own church. After Habsburg forces captured the town, that church was destroyed in 1686. A new church was permitted in 1695, and Patriarch Arsenije III Čarnojević renovated it in 1698. Hungarian Wikipedia says the new church of 1695 to 1698 stood on the foundations of a medieval church.
The Baroque church of 1733

A project for a new Baroque church was prepared in 1731, and Hungarian Wikipedia says the earlier church was demolished that year. The present church was built in 1733 to plans by András Mayerhoffer, an architect from Salzburg. The Baroque bell tower was completed in 1752, when the main facade also reached its present form. The Copf-style gate on Szerb utca was made in 1776. The original iconostasis was by Stefan Tenecki; after the flood of 1838 damaged it, a Neo-Renaissance iconostasis by a Greek artist was installed in 1850.
Change and survival in the twentieth century

In 1932 the street level was raised and a new wrought-iron gate was made, according to Hungarian Wikipedia. After the Second World War the community's more significant church, Saint Demetrius, was demolished in 1949 following war damage, which left the church on Szerb utca as the only Serbian place of worship in the city. In 1959 archaeological research confirmed that the present building stands on the site of an older church. The church is protected by the Hungarian National Office for Cultural Heritage and remains in use by the Eparchy of Buda.

introduction: The Queen of Heavens Church was built between 1875 and 1881 for a town that had been founded only in 1840. Its history follows Újpest's growth from a filial congregation to a main parish church.
chapters: A new town and its parish

Újpest was founded in 1840 on land given by Count István Károlyi, north of Pest. Until 1845 its Catholics were a filial of Dunakeszi, and then they were attached to the parish of Fót. In February 1870 Bishop Antal József Peitler of Vác made the Újpest congregation an independent parish. A parish house and a Catholic school were completed in 1873, and the parish was formally organised in 1875, with Vince Illek as its first pastor. He held the post until his death in 1905.
Building the church, 1875 to 1881

The church was built between 1875 and 1881, in the neo-Gothic style, to plans by József Kauser, with Károly Bachmann as builder. Two side aisles and a tower were added later to the original building. The tower is integral to the church and the aisles are joined to the main structure. Ferenc Walser cast the bells, three in 1888 and the largest, dedicated to King Saint Stephen, in 1924. A fifth, middle bell was lost in the Second World War.
The square and the district

The square in front of the church was called Templom tér, the Church Square, until it was named Szent István tér in 1928. It became the main square of Újpest after the town hall opened in 1900, and a Reformed church, built in 1878, stands on the same square. Újpest became part of Budapest in 1950, and in 1993 the parish passed from the Diocese of Vác to the Archdiocese of Esztergom-Budapest.

introduction: The Holy Family Church was built in 1930 and 1931, destroyed in large part on New Year's Day 1945 and rebuilt by 1948. Its history is the story of a district church that was built, lost its furnishings and was gradually refitted.
chapters: A church for the interwar city

Hungarian Wikipedia explains that Budapest's population grew significantly between the two world wars, which created the need for a new church at Szondi utca 67. The architect was Gáspár Fábián. The foundation stone was laid on 28 September 1930, and the church was consecrated on 15 November 1931 by the auxiliary bishop István Breyer. In 1933 the parish became a vicarage, and its first vicar, Ferenc Sármány, was also the builder of the church.
Destruction and reconstruction, 1945 to 1948

On 1 January 1945, during the Second World War, the church was struck and severely damaged. Hungarian Wikipedia speaks of a bomb, and the Budapest library's description of a chained explosive. The altars, pulpit, confessionals and lighting were destroyed, and the organ was partly destroyed. Only the crucifix beside the pulpit and a statue of Saint Thérèse of Lisieux survived. Reconstruction began in September 1947, and on 18 May 1948 Bishop Zoltán Meszlényi reconsecrated the church.
Refitting the church

In 1955 Zoltán Kodály, who visited the church often, paid for the marble cladding of the high altar and the pulpit. Péter Barba painted a secco in the sanctuary in 1961, and insulation work was carried out in the 1970s. A statue of the Rosa Mystica was installed in 1985, and a columbarium was built in the basement and courtyard in 1996. The church was renovated in 2000, two new bells were consecrated in 2002, Zsolt Boromisza painted two new seccos in 2003 and the organ was restored in 2006.

introduction: The Armenian Catholic church on Orlay utca grew out of a villa bought in the 1960s for Budapest's Hungarian-Armenian Catholics. Its history is tied to the Transylvanian Armenians who settled in the capital in the twentieth century.
chapters: A community that settled in Budapest

According to a study by the Budapest City Archives, most of the Armenians living in Budapest descend from the Hungarian-Armenian community of Transylvania. They arrived in a first wave among the civil servants of the period after 1850, and in a second wave after the First World War and the Treaty of Trianon, when many Hungarian Armenians who had lost their livelihoods moved to Hungary. The community then wanted its own church and its own priest. For a very long time, however, different Roman Catholic churches in Budapest hosted the Armenian Catholic community.
The villa on Orlay utca

The same study says that in the 1960s the Armenian Catholic Mechitarist priest Dániel Kádár started a fundraising effort, giving up his family's properties and collecting donations among Armenians in Hungary and in Western Europe. He succeeded in buying a villa on Orlay utca, where an Armenian Catholic pastoral office, a chapel, a museum and a library were set up. Interviews in the study describe the Orlay utca chapel as a place where people felt at home, as in a second family.
Renovation of the parish centre

In November 2022 the renovated Armenian parish centre in Budapest was inaugurated. The National Catholic Register reported that Cardinal Péter Erdő and the Armenian Catholic Patriarch Raphaël Bedros XXI Minassian blessed the premises and that the Hungarian government paid for the renovation through the Hungary Helps Program. The renovated section is intended to host educational and cultural projects and the archives of the Hungarian-Armenian community.

introduction: The Pozsonyi úti Reformed Church was built between 1936 and 1940 for a congregation that had outgrown its first meeting house. Its history includes severe war damage in 1944 and a rescue effort in its basement.
chapters: From Tutaj utca to a design competition

The Reformed congregation first met at the corner of Tutaj utca and Visegrádi utca, and the parish website says its first permanent meeting house on Tutaj utca was consecrated in 1926. It outgrew that site and received a new plot from the municipality, on marshy ground. A design competition was announced in 1935. Imre Tóth won first place and Jenő Halászy second, and both took part in the construction. Lajos Simkovics, a civil engineer, supervised the works.
Building the Thanksgiving church, 1936 to 1940

Work began on 6 December 1936 with a thanksgiving service on the empty plot, and the foundation stone was laid on 25 April 1937, with Bishop László Ravasz recorded by the parish as laying it. The ground was raised with soil and more than three hundred piles were driven. Construction took about four years because of stoppages caused by the approaching war, shortages of money and sulfurous water that surfaced from the ground, which forced a redesign, especially of the tower, which stands on pile foundations. The church was consecrated on 8 December 1940, before the Second World War broke out.
War damage and restoration

The church came through most of the war largely unscathed but was severely damaged in 1944, standing between German artillery fire from Buda and Soviet fire from Pest. The Danube-side entrance, part of the colonnade and the organ were hit, and damage marks remained visible until 1972, when the building was restored. After the war the basement served as a warehouse for about fifty years and was later returned to use as a theatre. Parish information says repairs were completed by 1972, and a destroyed facade pillar was restored for the church's fiftieth anniversary.

stories.title: Hiding in the basement
description: WeLoveBudapest reports that during the later war years the basement of the church sheltered deserters, wanted resistance members and mainly Jewish families who had false papers. Pastor Albert Bereczky, who had led the church's construction, and members of his congregation were involved.

According to the article, the basement had its own toilet, so those hiding did not need to come up, they received food, and a child was born there. No one was discovered by the Germans, the Arrow Cross or the Soviets. Bereczky received the Righteous Among the Nations award.
stories.sourceLabel: WeLoveBudapest: history of the Pozsonyi úti Hálaadás church

introduction: Rumbach Street Synagogue was built for the Status Quo Ante community in the early 1870s and then spent decades in decay before a restoration that ended in 2021. Its history follows the changing fortunes of Jewish Pest.
chapters: Building for the Status Quo Ante, 1869 to 1873

English Wikipedia says the building was begun in 1869, during the schism in Hungarian Jewry, and Hungarian Wikipedia gives the start of construction as 1 May 1870, with the Jewish congregation applying for the building permit only on 14 June 1870. Otto Wagner designed the synagogue, and the work was funded by public donations. The prayer space was consecrated on 1 October 1872, and the use permit was issued on 10 May 1873. It was intended for traditionalist Jews who found the Neolog synagogues too liberal.
War and decay, 1941 to the 1980s

In 1941 Jews were gathered in the building before Hungarian authorities deported them to Kamianets-Podilskyi in occupied Ukraine, where Germans murdered them. A plaque commemorates them. During the Second World War only the residential part of the building suffered minor damage. After 1956 about eighty congregants remained, and the synagogue was no longer used for worship from 1959. In 1979 the roof above the Torah ark collapsed, and the women's gallery later collapsed as well. The building was declared life-threatening and evacuated in 1980, and unknown perpetrators looted it in 1982.
Ownership and restoration, 1980s to 2021

In the 1980s a state construction company bought the building from the congregation, and in the 1990s preservation work restored the sanctuary but left the renovation unfinished. The Mazsihisz Jewish federation received the building in 2005, and from 2006 it was open to visitors without its interior fittings. Works began in 2017, designed by the König-Wagner office on the basis of Wagner's surviving plans and historic photographs, and the Hungarian ICOMOS committee gave the restoration an award in 2019. The renovated building was officially opened on 10 June 2021.

introduction: The Kazinczy Street Synagogue was built in 1912 and 1913 for Pest's Orthodox Jewish community, after a design competition that the congregation decided against its jury. Its history runs through war damage, decline and a long search for a way to keep the community worshipping.
chapters: The competition of 1909 and 1910

Hungarian Wikipedia says the idea of an Orthodox synagogue in Erzsébetváros emerged in 1909, on a site on Kazinczy utca that belonged to the Pest Autonomous Orthodox Congregation. A design competition was announced on 25 June 1909. The jury chose the design of József Porgesz and Sándor Skultetzky, but in May 1910 the congregation overruled it and selected the design of the brothers Sándor and Béla Löffler. The budget was 650,000 korona, and the detailed plans were approved on 8 November 1910.
Construction, 1911 to 1913

The school and the community headquarters of the complex were completed in 1911 and handed over in 1912. Work on the synagogue began in the spring of 1912. In July 1913, because of delays and unexpected costs, the Löffler brothers submitted a revised, plainer facade with lower material costs. The official use permit was issued on 29 September 1913. A mikveh, or ritual bath, began operating in the building in 1928.
War, decline and repairs

In 1944 and 1945 the building lay in the Budapest ghetto area. It was damaged in the Second World War and part of the furnishings was destroyed, and the complex was restored and the furnishings reconstructed after 1945. In the following decades the main synagogue deteriorated, and by the end of the twentieth century it was unheatable and unsafe. The congregation then used the ground floor of a neighbouring teacher-training college, now part of ELTE, and a small modern prayer house built in the corner of the site by the engineer Sándor Bokor. The mikveh reopened in 2004 after renovation funded by private donations.

introduction: The Frankel Leó Street Synagogue was consecrated in 1888 as the Újlak Synagogue and was later enclosed by a residential building. It has served an active congregation through war, socialism and a renovation in 2000.
chapters: The synagogue of 1888

Hungarian Wikipedia records that the foundation stone was laid in 1887, the building was completed in 1888 and it was consecrated on 8 August 1888. Sándor Fellner designed it in the neo-Gothic style, and it replaced an earlier synagogue that was about a hundred years old. It was originally freestanding, with its entrance facing what was then Zsigmond utca, now Frankel Leó út. Single-storey houses, a kosher butcher shop and community apartments stood around it, and it was built for about 400 worshippers.
The residential building of 1928

In the 1920s a residential building was constructed around the synagogue. It was handed over on 1 August 1928, designed by Dezső Jakab and his son-in-law Aladár Sós on the initiative of a former community president, Berthold Beer. At the same time the synagogue itself was rebuilt, with reinforced concrete floor slabs, and was joined to the residential building.
War, socialism and renovation

At the end of the Second World War the synagogue was used as a stable, and the Jewish residents of the building were deported in 1944. A black marble plaque in the courtyard, unveiled in 2014 for the seventieth anniversary, commemorates them. The residential building and the synagogue survived the siege of Budapest almost intact. Under socialism the synagogue functioned again as a prayer house, and in 2000 it was completely renovated. Today it belongs to the Buda Jewish Community, which follows the Ashkenazi prayer rite.
